Mandarin: 通常朋友聽到我是客家人，就會開始聯想到刻板印象比如節儉、勤奮等，比如從小就被教育碗裡的東西要吃乾淨，不能浪費水浪費電，但離開台灣後就比較少人知道這些了。到紐約時除了食物以外，沒有再有意識的接觸客家相關的東西，我覺得我正在融入一個新的文化，而客家這個身份離我變得遙遠，像是在老相簿偶然翻到會想起來的我的一部分。直到在一個活動上偶然遇到同鄉人才討論起客家的事，從來沒有想過人在異鄉，「客家」會成為聯繫我們的關鍵字，而這個久未聽到，卻深植在我靈魂的身份，意外地喚醒了我對於自己身份的好奇與重新探索。
English:
When friends learn that I’m Hakka, they often bring up the usual stereotypes—thriftiness, hard work, and frugality. I did grow up being told to finish every grain of rice in my bowl and to never waste water or electricity. But after leaving Taiwan, I found that few people outside the country knew about any of this.
When I moved to New York, apart from food, I rarely encountered anything related to Hakka culture. I felt myself blending into a new world, while my Hakka identity began to fade into the background, like an old photograph tucked away in an album, something I’d only recall once in a while.
Then one day, at a community event, I met another Hakka by chance. We started talking, and it struck me how this word, Hakka, became an instant bridge between two strangers in a foreign place. Hearing it again, after so long, stirred something deep inside me. It reignited a quiet curiosity about who I am, and what it really means to carry this identity across distance and time.
